questions.prompt: Explain why linked list nodes in Swift must be classes rather than structs, and describe what happens if you try to make them structs. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, structs are value types that must have a fixed byte size calculated at compile time. If a struct contains an unboxed property of its own type, it would require infinite memory to store nested instances. The Swift compiler detects this recursive dependency and throws a fatal compile-time error. Using classes solves this because reference pointers have a fixed 64-bit size.

questions.prompt: Explain the 3-pointer algorithm for reversing a singly-linked list in-place and state its time and space complexities. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: To reverse a singly-linked list in-place, initialize prev to nil and curr to head. In a loop, cache curr.next in a temporary variable. Redirect curr.next to point backward to prev. Then advance prev to curr and curr to the cached next node. The loop repeats until curr becomes nil, returning prev as the new head. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

rubric.criterion: Describes the roles of prev, curr, and temporary next pointers during reversal.
Explains that caching next before rewiring curr.next preserves access to the rest of the list.
States the correct O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space complexities.

questions.prompt: Explain how Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm detects a loop in a linked list and why === is required in Swift. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: Floyd's algorithm uses two pointers: slow moves forward one node per step while fast moves forward two nodes per step. If a cycle exists, the fast pointer enters the loop and must eventually catch up to the slow pointer from behind. When slow and fast meet, a cycle is confirmed. In Swift, we compare slow === fast to verify that both pointers reference the exact same memory address rather than different nodes with equal values.

rubric.criterion: Explains the two-pointer speed difference (slow moves 1, fast moves 2).
States that fast will lap slow if a cycle exists.
Explains that === checks reference instance identity rather than value equality.

questions.prompt: Why is a dummy head node useful in linked list problems, and how does it simplify edge cases? Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: A dummy head is a temporary sentinel node whose next pointer references the actual list head. It eliminates special-case branching when inserting before the head or deleting the head node. All mutations can be treated as operations following an existing node without separate if-checks for empty lists or new heads. When finished, returning dummy.next yields the updated list cleanly.

rubric.criterion: Defines a dummy node as a temporary sentinel placed before the actual head.
Explains that it avoids special conditionals for modifying or removing the first node.
Notes that returning dummy.next provides the final list head cleanly.

questions.prompt: Explain what causes call stack overflow when deallocating deep linked lists in Swift and how to resolve it. Write 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.modelAnswer: When a linked list head is deallocated in Swift, Automatic Reference Counting recursively releases its next child node. If the list contains tens of thousands of nodes, each release adds a stack frame to the call stack. This chain can exhaust thread stack memory and trigger a stack overflow crash. To prevent this, implement an iterative loop in deinit that breaks child next pointers one by one.

rubric.criterion: Explains that ARC recursively releases child nodes upon deallocation.

Proposes an iterative deallocation loop inside deinit to flatten the cleanup.
